p: The Hoo Peninsula is one of Kent's least-known corners, a flat stretch of farmland, creeks and grazing marsh between the Thames and the Medway. It's quiet, open and big-skied, and it's a fantastic place for anyone who loves wildlife.

A short drive from St Mary Hoo, the RSPB reserve at Northward Hill near High Halstow is known for its heronry, one of the largest in the country, set in woodland overlooking the marshes. Spring is the best time to see the nests. Over at Cliffe, the RSPB's Cliffe Pools reserve is a patchwork of lagoons that attracts wading birds and wildfowl in big numbers, and the trails are mostly flat.

Charles Dickens knew these marshes well, and the churchyard at Cooling is said to have inspired the opening of Great Expectations, where young Pip meets the convict Magwitch. The rows of tiny gravestones there are a moving sight. Nearby, Upnor Castle, an Elizabethan fort on the bank of the Medway, faces Chatham Dockyard across the water and is a good stop for history buffs.

Practical bits: public transport on the peninsula is limited, so you'll want a car. Pack wellies or boots if you're planning to walk the marshes, and binoculars if you've got them. Pubs and cafés are thin on the ground, so combining the animals with a meal at the inn is a sensible plan.
